learning.concept: Permit the return direction using the actual destination ports and client CIDR at a stateless subnet boundary.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Evaluate user-supplied text without scanning trusted instructions as input
prompt: A text assistant uses a supported Bedrock InvokeModel integration. Its request concatenates developer instructions and user-provided task text. The team has configured a Guardrails prompt attack filter and wants it applied to the user-provided segment separately from the developer's instructions. Which integration meets the requirement?

choices.text: Tag only the developer instructions and leave the user-provided segment outside the evaluated content.
choices.explanation: This evaluates the wrong part of the prompt and leaves the intended segment outside the scoped check.

choices.text: Pass the permitted guardrail configuration and tag the user-provided segment with the documented guard-content input tags.
choices.explanation: The integration can scope the prompt attack check to that selected content segment.

choices.text: Run only an output profanity policy after generation.
choices.explanation: An output policy that checks profanity does not apply the requested input prompt attack evaluation.

choices.text: Replace the explicit guardrail check with a longer system instruction telling the model to trust only developers.
choices.explanation: Prompt wording does not configure or prove execution of the guardrail filter on the selected input.

learning.reason: Supported input tagging identifies the content span to evaluate. The prompt attack filter can target user input without treating the developer's own system instructions as untrusted input.
learning.concept: Identify untrusted content precisely at the guardrail boundary for the prompt attack check.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Attribute agent costs during long waits for tools
prompt: AgentCore Runtime traces show that an agent spends much of each active session waiting for remote tool responses. No background CPU work occurs during those waits, but the runtime retains a large heap and remains alive. The team uses consumption-based pricing. Which cost hypothesis should it investigate first?

choices.text: Treat every second of tool wait as fully utilized CPU and ignore memory.
choices.explanation: The consumption model does not treat blocked I/O as active CPU when there is no other processing.

choices.text: Assume neither CPU nor retained memory can incur any cost while a session awaits an external response.
choices.explanation: The memory can remain in use throughout the active runtime's wait.

choices.text: Check memory footprint and time retained during the waits because CPU can be idle while memory cost persists.
choices.explanation: Separating the resource dimensions shows how slower external tools can raise retained memory time even without active CPU work.

choices.text: Assume the tool's external token cost is included in one fixed runtime fee.
choices.explanation: External model and tool costs are separate from the runtime's CPU and memory accounting.

learning.reason: AgentCore Runtime accounts for active CPU and retained memory separately. An I/O wait can leave CPU idle while memory remains allocated and billable for the living runtime.
learning.concept: Attribute tool-wait cost to the appropriate resources rather than treating elapsed time as fully busy CPU.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Replace a manifest encryption key without breaking historical reads
prompt: An application encrypts small manifests directly with a symmetric AWS KMS key referenced by an alias. The security team wants new writes to use a different KMS key. Existing ciphertext must remain readable until it is migrated; no old key compromise is suspected. What should the application owners do? (Choose two.)

choices.text: Change the alias and immediately schedule deletion of the original key without migrating the stored manifests.
choices.explanation: Old manifests can become unreadable because their ciphertext still depends on that key.

choices.text: Create or select the permitted replacement key and point the existing encryption alias at it for new writes.
choices.explanation: New encrypt operations using the alias can target the replacement key without changing callers' alias configuration.

choices.text: Tell the application to decrypt each old ciphertext using the new key's ARN as if the alias changed the key referenced by the blob.
choices.explanation: The new key cannot decrypt historical ciphertext created under a different key.

choices.text: Copy the encrypted manifest objects to another prefix without re-encrypting their ciphertext and then disable the original key.
choices.explanation: The location change does not replace the key dependency of the copied ciphertext.

choices.text: Keep the old key available for authorized old reads until historical ciphertext has been re-encrypted or no longer needs to be retained.
choices.explanation: Changing the alias does not migrate ciphertext already protected by the original key.

learning.reason: Moving an alias directs future key lookups to a new key. Old ciphertext still depends on the original key, so historical reads need old-key access until validated re-encryption or retention expiry.
learning.concept: Separate alias redirection for new encryption from the lifetime of the key that protects existing ciphertext.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Limit one queue's share of a common inference worker
prompt: Two standard SQS queues invoke the same Lambda inference worker. Low-priority replay must use at most five concurrent invocations, while the urgent queue needs up to 15 through that same function. The function has reserved concurrency of 20, and event source provisioned mode is off. Which change enforces separate queue limits?

choices.text: Set the function's reserved concurrency to five and leave both mappings unconstrained.
choices.explanation: The shared function cap also restricts urgent work to at most five concurrent invocations.

choices.text: Set the replay queue's message batch size to five and leave mapping concurrency unspecified.
choices.explanation: Batch size controls records per invocation, not how many concurrent invocations the mapping starts.

choices.text: Set the replay message visibility timeout to five seconds and assume only five Lambda executions will run.
choices.explanation: Queue invisibility duration is unrelated to a concurrent execution cap and can cause extra processing if too short.

choices.text: Set MaximumConcurrency to five on the replay mapping and 15 on the urgent mapping, keeping sufficient function concurrency.
choices.explanation: Each queue is independently constrained and the aggregate function capacity can accommodate both limits.

learning.reason: Maximum concurrency on each SQS event source mapping limits simultaneous function invocations from that source. Function reserved concurrency bounds the shared function as a whole.
learning.concept: Apply source-specific concurrency limits when the shared function ceiling cannot distinguish queues.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Detect failed tool work when the transport request succeeds
prompt: An agent's MCP client gets successful HTTP responses and JSON-RPC result objects, but an inventory tool sometimes cannot complete its lookup. The tool reports these failures in the documented result field. The operations team needs separate counts for connectivity issues and tool failures. What should it count?

choices.text: Count results with isError set to true as tool failures and keep a separate series for transport and protocol failures.
choices.explanation: This catches the failed lookups without mislabeling successful delivery of a tool error as a broken connection.

choices.text: Count every successful HTTP response as a successful lookup, regardless of its result fields.
choices.explanation: A valid exchange can carry the tool's failure rather than a completed lookup.

choices.text: Mark every returned text block as a failure, since working tools always return a binary result.
choices.explanation: Tools can return text as ordinary successful content. The explicit error flag carries the needed status.

choices.text: Count only failures to connect and infer their rate is also the application's tool failure rate.
choices.explanation: Tool-level errors can occur on healthy connections and would be missed.

source.label: Model Context Protocol TypeScript SDK documentation

learning.reason: MCP distinguishes a failed tool execution marked in a valid result from a transport or protocol failure. An error inside the result must be counted even if the exchange succeeded.
learning.concept: Observe the tool outcome as well as the protocol exchange when measuring agent reliability.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Recover historical ML spend attribution after late billing activation
prompt: A management account activated the CostCenter cost allocation tag this month. The tag had already been assigned to supported training resources during the past eight months, but the historical report does not show those tag values. The account can request a backfill and wants the analysis to acknowledge any historical resources that were never tagged. Which expectation is correct?

choices.text: Set current CostCenter values on all resources and assume the backfill projects today's values onto every past charge.
choices.explanation: Tag history constrains what the backfill can report. A current label alone does not create a historical one.

choices.text: Request a backfill from within the supported window and reconcile historical allocations only where the resource already had the tag.
choices.explanation: The backfill applies billing activation retrospectively; it cannot add a tag value that did not exist then.

choices.text: Create a new tag key and expect it to recover the earlier CostCenter values automatically.
choices.explanation: The new key has no historical assignments for the pipeline's prior spend.

choices.text: Conclude that historical visibility is impossible any time activation happens after the billing month.
choices.explanation: The supported backfill can recover eligible historical data under the stated conditions.

learning.reason: AWS Billing can backfill a tag's activation within its supported lookback period. Cost data can show historical values only for resources that actually had the tag at the time.
learning.concept: Recover late-activated attribution from historical tag assignments and avoid inventing tags for untagged spend.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Supply provider evidence for a model platform audit
prompt: An internal audit asks for the AWS provider's current independent compliance reports for underlying cloud services and separate evidence that the company's ML application enforces its own access requirements. Which approach addresses those two evidence sources?

choices.text: Download an AWS Artifact report and treat it as proof every identity policy in the application follows least privilege.
choices.explanation: Provider reports do not test the customer's specific policy or application configuration.

choices.text: Submit only application metrics to prove the AWS provider met its independent audit scope.
choices.explanation: Local metrics do not substitute for the provider's audited service report.

choices.text: Retrieve the relevant provider reports from AWS Artifact and collect separate application evidence such as authorization tests and deployment audit records.
choices.explanation: The two evidence sources address the service provider and the customer's workload responsibilities respectively.

choices.text: Use billing invoices as the sole proof of both infrastructure controls and application access decisions.
choices.explanation: A billing record does not establish either set of security controls.

learning.reason: AWS Artifact supplies provider security and compliance reports. Those reports are evidence about AWS services, while the customer gathers controls evidence for its own workload.
learning.concept: Use provider audit documents for the AWS side and independent customer evidence for application controls.

category: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
examDomain: Operating, Monitoring, and Securing ML and AI Solutions
title: Reserve matching inference capacity in the required failover zone
prompt: An EC2-hosted inference service must launch a known instance type in one designated Availability Zone during regional recovery drills. Other workloads with the same instance type run in that account and must not consume the reserved slots. The team is willing to pay for held capacity. Which configuration meets the requirement?

choices.text: Buy a Compute Savings Plan and launch into any Availability Zone using the standard launch settings.
choices.explanation: A pricing commitment does not itself hold a slot in the required zone.

choices.text: Create an open reservation in the target zone and allow any matching launch to consume it.
choices.explanation: Other workloads may use an open reservation if they match its attributes.

choices.text: Create a targeted reservation for a similar type in a different Availability Zone and reference it from the required zone.
choices.explanation: A Capacity Reservation does not supply capacity across a mismatch in zone or instance type.

choices.text: Create a targeted On-Demand Capacity Reservation with the matching type, platform, tenancy, and Availability Zone, and configure recovery launches to target it.
choices.explanation: The slots are allocated to launches that explicitly use the targeted reservation and match its capacity properties.

learning.reason: A targeted On-Demand Capacity Reservation holds matching capacity in its Availability Zone for launches that select it. Matching attributes and explicit targeting matter independently of discounts.
learning.concept: Protect dedicated zonal launch capacity from matching but unrelated workloads.
